design_detail: Brief report of a randomized, double-blind, saline-controlled, two-period crossover trial by a Connecticut (USA) group (Connecticut Mental Health Center, West Haven VA Medical Center, Yale; number of sites not stated). 9 medication-free adults with a DSM-IV major depressive episode were to have two test days at least 1 week apart, in random order: an intravenous infusion over 40 minutes of ketamine hydrochloride (total 0.5 mg/kg) on one day and of saline alone on the other, following the procedure of Krystal et al. (1994). Ratings: 25-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) from baseline to 72 hours, Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) to 72 hours, and a visual analogue scale for feeling 'high' and the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) during the first 2 to 4 hours. Repeated-measures ANOVA (condition × time) on the 7 who completed both days; response (a 50% or greater HDRS fall within 3 days) counted in the 8 who had each condition. Setting (inpatient or outpatient) not stated; no registration or protocol mentioned.
can_establish: Whether, in 7 medication-free adults with a major depressive episode who completed both test days, depression ratings over the 3 days after one 40-minute intravenous infusion of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg differed from those after a saline infusion, and how self-rated 'high' and BPRS positive symptoms changed in the first hours after it.
cannot_establish: Whether the antidepressant effect is specific rather than driven by expectation (saline has none of ketamine's perceptible effects, and the authors say patients readily told the infusions apart); its size free of carryover (washout at least 1 week, while the effect is said to last 1 to 2 weeks) and of a 6-point higher baseline before ketamine; its duration beyond 72 hours (later observations lie outside the rating schedule); effects in treatment-resistant depression as such (treatment history is not reported); any cognitive effect (no cognitive test was given); and any harm rarer than 9 people treated once can show.

sample.recruitment: Not reported. Authors' units: Clinical Neuroscience Research Unit of the Connecticut Mental Health Center (New Haven), Affective Disorders Program of the West Haven VA Medical Center, and the Department of Psychiatry, Yale University; approval by the IRB of the VA Connecticut Healthcare system, West Haven campus (pp. 351–352).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV major depressive episode by the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (8 recurrent unipolar major depression, 1 bipolar disorder, depressed); no recent diagnosis of alcohol or substance abuse (2 had a history of alcohol abuse in remission for more than 8 years); no lifetime diagnosis of another Axis I disorder except 1 person with comorbid panic disorder; drug-free, in good health and unmedicated for at least 2 weeks before the first test day, by history, physical examination, routine blood tests, electrocardiogram, urinalysis and urine toxicology (pp. 351–352). No severity threshold, treatment-resistance criterion or exclusion of psychotic features is stated.
sample.demographics: 4 men, 5 women; age 37 (SD 10), range 23–56; 2 Hispanic, 7 Caucasian (p. 351). Baseline 25-item HDRS 33.0 (SD 6.7) before ketamine and 26.9 (SD 5.8) before saline; BDI 29.5 (SD 8.2) and 23.0 (SD 8.2) (pp. 352–353). Illness duration, episode length and prior treatments are not reported.
sample.attrition: 2 of 9 left before their second test day, one after the ketamine day and one after the saline day, to start antidepressant treatment; both were excluded from the ANOVAs (pp. 351–352). The person who had only the ketamine day went from HDRS 33 to 16 (p. 352). The response counts use the 8 people who had each condition (p. 353).
sample.selection_effects: Very small sample of unstated origin; people willing to stay off medication for at least 2 weeks and to accept a challenge described to them at consent as possibly worsening their depression and causing distressing cognitive disturbances (p. 352). Diagnoses are mixed (one bipolar depression, one comorbid panic disorder), treatment history is unknown, and the main analysis keeps completers only.

exposure.measurement: Assigned infusion, ketamine hydrochloride or saline, given under randomized double-blind conditions as described in Krystal et al. (1994); how the solutions were prepared, who gave them and how the blind was kept are not described in this report (p. 352). No blood levels were measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: ketamine hydrochloride, total dose 0.5 mg/kg, infused intravenously over 40 minutes, once; saline alone infused the same way on the other test day; the two test days at least 1 week apart (p. 352).
exposure.polysubstance: A recent alcohol or substance abuse diagnosis was an exclusion; 2 participants had alcohol abuse in remission for more than 8 years; urine toxicology at screening (pp. 351–352). Tobacco, caffeine and current alcohol use are not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Drug-free and unmedicated for at least 2 weeks before the first test day, checked by history and urine toxicology (p. 352). Whether participants stayed off medication between test days is not stated, except that the 2 who left did so to begin antidepressants.

comparison.controls: Each completer's own saline test day: an inert placebo without ketamine's perceptible effects; no active control.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; order randomized, with 4 assigned ketamine first (p. 352). Baseline HDRS was 33.0 before ketamine and 26.9 before saline (paired t test, p = 0.10), and the second test day began lower than the first by 10.3 points (SD 9.0) when ketamine came first and by 3.0 points (SD 7.5) when saline came first (p = .29) (p. 352). Neither difference was adjusted for.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a between-group comparison; but illness history, previous treatments and participants' expectations were not recorded, and no first-period-only analysis is reported to separate the treatment effect from period and carryover effects.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (same people on both days).

outcomes.instruments: 25-item HDRS (clinician-rated depression severity) at baseline and 80 min, 230 min, 24 h, 48 h and 72 h after the start of infusion; BDI (self-rated depression) at the same times plus 10, 40 and 110 min after infusion; visual analogue scale for feeling 'high' (VAS-high, self-rated intoxication, 0–100 mm) at baseline and 10, 40, 80 and 110 min after infusion; BPRS (clinician-rated psychiatric symptoms, analysed as the positive-symptom score) at baseline and 10, 40, 80, 110 and 230 min after infusion (p. 352). VAS-high and BPRS therefore cover the infusion and the following hours; HDRS and BDI cover the 3 days after it. Whether the times 'after infusion' count from its start or its end is stated only for the HDRS (from the start).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments. The BPRS version and the items making up its positive-symptom score are not given.
outcomes.operationalization: Antidepressant effect: the condition × time interaction on HDRS and BDI totals. Response: a 50% or greater HDRS decrease 'during the 3-day follow-up period', without saying whether at 72 h or at any rating (p. 353). Return to baseline: clinical impression and HDRS within 5 points of baseline, observed 1 to 2 weeks after infusion, outside the stated rating schedule (p. 353). Psychotomimetic effects: VAS-high and BPRS positive symptoms. No cognitive test was given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four repeated-measures ANOVAs (HDRS, BDI, VAS-high, BPRS-positive) with Huynh-Feldt correction for sphericity only; post hoc contrasts at each time point against baseline and between conditions (Figure 1); a Fisher exact test of response; two correlations; and paired t tests on individual HDRS items (number of items tested not stated), stated to be uncorrected for multiple comparisons (pp. 352–353).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Described as double-blind. Who rated the HDRS and BPRS is not stated and no check of blinding was made; the authors write that patients readily told the active infusion from placebo by its perceptual disturbances and 'high' (p. 353).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported. HDRS (7 completers): condition × time F = 3.97, df 5,30, p = .02; time F = 2.62, p = .09; condition F = 0.157, p = .71 (p. 352). Abstract: HDRS fell by 14 (SD 10) points within 72 hours after ketamine and by 0 (SD 12) after saline (p. 351). BDI: ketamine day 29.5 (SD 8.2) at baseline to 16.8 (SD 10.5); saline day 23.0 (SD 8.2) to 25.2 (SD 6.0); drug × time F = 5.7, df 8,48, p = .0001 (p. 353). Response: 4 of 8 after ketamine against 1 of 8 after saline, Fisher exact p > .05 (p. 353). VAS-high condition × time F = 16.9, df 4,24, p = .0001; BPRS-positive condition × time F = 4.14, df 5,30, p = .068 (p. 353). Editors' calculations: standardized difference in HDRS change about 1.3 (14 against 0 points, pooled SD about 11, treating the two conditions as independent because the SD of within-person differences is not reported); response difference 37.5 percentage points (95% CI about −7 to 68, Newcombe method, conditions treated as independent), two-sided Fisher exact p = 0.28.
analysis.covariates: None. Baseline differences between test days and treatment order were not adjusted for; order effects were examined post hoc only (p > .3) (p. 353).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or named primary outcome is mentioned; the abstract leads with the HDRS change.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives the HDRS change but not the non-significant response comparison. The BPRS paragraph opens by calling the BPRS rise significant, while every BPRS-positive test printed is not (p = .06 to .10); BPRS totals are not shown. HDRS item tests are reported only for the items that changed after ketamine. The timing of 'response' and the method of the post hoc between-condition contrasts are not described.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. 7 completers.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 7 completers, HDRS and BDI scores fell over the 3 days after the ketamine infusion and not after saline (condition × time p = .02 and p = .0001). 4 of 8 people reached a 50% HDRS fall after ketamine against 1 of 8 after saline, a difference that was not significant. Self-rated 'high' peaked during or just after the infusion and was gone by 110 minutes; BPRS positive-symptom scores were higher in the first 80 minutes or so and back near baseline by 110 minutes, without a significant condition × time effect. Baseline depression was higher before ketamine than before saline, the second test day started lower than the first in both orders, and the authors state that patients could tell the infusions apart.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the study "the first placebo-controlled, double-blinded trial" of a single NMDA-antagonist dose in depression and reports significant improvement within 72 hours (p. 351). The Discussion speaks of 'robust decreases' in depressive symptoms, reads the item results as a lessening of core symptoms and the timing as showing that the improvement is disconnected from the 'high', and says ketamine induced "profound and transient cognitive deficits" as shown by BPRS increases (p. 353). Gaps: (1) 'double-blinded' stands against the authors' own statement that patients readily recognized the active infusion; (2) 'robust' rests on 7 completers, a non-significant response comparison and a 6-point higher baseline before ketamine; (3) no cognitive test was given and the BPRS-positive effect was not significant; (4) the separation from the 'high' rests on two null correlations in 7 or 8 people; (5) the 1-to-2-week duration comes from observations outside the stated rating schedule. In the authors' favour, the Discussion names the unblinding as a possible confound and the psychotomimetic effects and potential for abuse as limits to clinical use (p. 353), and the conclusion in the abstract is worded as suggesting a potential role.

timeline.event: Krystal et al.: the healthy-volunteer study from the same group whose infusion procedure and rating times this trial follows (p. 352).

Zarate et al.: crossover trial in 18 inpatients with treatment-resistant unipolar depression, the same 0.5 mg/kg infusion against saline, 1 week apart; HDRS lower from 110 minutes to day 7, with carryover into the saline period (as recorded on this round's first-pass card sc_zarate_2006).

Murrough et al.: two-site parallel trial, 72 analysed, the same dose against midazolam as an active placebo; MADRS 7.95 points lower at 24 hours and response 30 of 47 against 7 of 25 (as recorded on this round's first-pass card sc_murrough_2013). Dennis S. Charney is an author of Berman et al. (2000), Zarate et al. (2006) and Murrough et al. (2013) (reference records).

Short et al.: systematic review of side-effects in 60 depression studies of ketamine, listing this trial first among 20 randomized trials, with short-term BPRS and VAS ratings and 7 patients given ketamine.

Anand et al.: randomized noninferiority trial of six infusions of the same dose (0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, twice weekly for 3 weeks) against ECT in 365 analysed patients; self-rated response 55.4% against 41.2%. Amit Anand is an author of both trials.

replication.where_it_stands: A fall in depression ratings in the first days after one 0.5 mg/kg infusion was found again against saline in a larger crossover trial (Zarate et al., 2006) and against an active placebo in a parallel trial (Murrough et al., 2013); both share investigators with this group. This pilot cannot by itself be cited for the size or the duration of the effect: its estimate rests on 7 completers, an inert placebo with acknowledged unblinding, baseline imbalance and probable carryover.

funding.funder: Supported in part by a Donaghue Foundation (RMB), a Merit Review Grant from the Department of Veterans Affairs (DSC, JHK) and a VA-Yale Alcoholism Research Center; research supported by a VA Merit Award (NNB), an NIMH Program Grant and the State of Connecticut (acknowledgement note, p. 353).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Academic and VA units in Connecticut; no industry support is declared. The initials NNB in the funding note match none of the seven authors. The infusion procedure is the one this group published in healthy volunteers (Krystal et al., 1994). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A parallel-group trial, or a crossover with a washout longer than the effect, using an active placebo that mimics ketamine's acute perceptible effects; a registered primary outcome at a fixed time; raters kept apart from the infusion sessions; a check of what patients and raters guessed; analysis adjusted for baseline; and ratings on a fixed schedule beyond 72 hours.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two infusions)
domains.note: Order was randomized (4 assigned ketamine first), but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described, and first-period baselines by order are not reported. Over both periods, baseline HDRS was 6.1 points higher before ketamine (p = 0.10).

The washout was at least 1 week, while the authors say the improvement lasted 1 to 2 weeks; the second test day began 10.3 points lower than the first when ketamine came first. No first-period analysis or period term is reported, only a post hoc order test in 7 people (p > .3), which has little power to detect carryover.

Saline has none of ketamine's acute effects, and the authors state that patients readily identified the active infusion; how this may have changed behaviour or care is not reported. Whether medication stayed off between test days is not stated.

2 of 9 (22%) missed a test day and were dropped from the ANOVAs; both left to start antidepressants, a reason linked to their depression, and the one with only the ketamine day had improved (HDRS 33 to 16). The response count includes 8 per condition, which partly offsets this.

HDRS (clinician-rated) and BDI (self-rated) are subjective; patients could tell the infusions apart, and raters seeing them during the session probably could too; no blinding check. The consent information warned that the challenge might worsen depression, which runs against a simple expectancy account but does not remove the bias.

No protocol or registered outcome. Many time points and four scales; the response definition does not fix a time; HDRS item tests reported selectively and uncorrected; the abstract omits the non-significant response comparison.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized within-person design and a significant condition × time interaction on two depression scales make a short-term difference between ketamine and saline days likely in these 7 people. The overall judgment is high because the outcomes are subjective ratings under an inert placebo that the authors say patients saw through, because the washout was shorter than the reported duration of benefit and the baselines differed by order and condition, and because the sample is tiny with completers-only analysis. The source can be cited as an early placebo-controlled report (by the authors' account the first) of lower depression ratings within 72 hours after one 0.5 mg/kg infusion, and for the time course of the self-rated 'high' (gone by 110 minutes); the BPRS-positive rise in the first hour was not significant on the interaction test and should be cited only as such; it cannot be cited for the size of the antidepressant effect, its specificity beyond expectation, its duration beyond 72 hours, response rates, or any cognitive effect.

key_findings.finding: 9 adults with a DSM-IV major depressive episode (8 recurrent unipolar, 1 bipolar, depressed) entered; 2 left before their second test day, one after ketamine and one after saline, to start antidepressant treatment, leaving 7 who completed both days for the ANOVAs. The person excluded after the ketamine day only went from HDRS 33 to 16.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 351, right column, continued on p. 352); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 352, left column)

key_findings.finding: Study conditions: two test days at least 1 week apart in randomized, double-blind order; saline alone or ketamine hydrochloride, total dose 0.5 mg/kg, infused intravenously over 40 minutes; 4 participants were randomly assigned ketamine first.
HDRS (25-item), 7 completers: significant condition × time interaction (F = 3.97, df 5,30, p = .02), with no significant effect of time (F = 2.62, df 5,30, p = .09) or condition (F = 0.157, p = .71).
key_findings.note: The condition df is printed as 1,30; see reporting issue 1.

key_findings.finding: The abstract summarizes the HDRS result as a fall of 14 (SD 10) points within 72 hours after ketamine against 0 (SD 12) after saline.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (p. 352; editors' reading of the plotted means, approximate) shows a mean change of about −8 points at 230 minutes, −11 at 24 hours, −13 at 48 hours and −13 at 72 hours after ketamine, against values between about −2 and +2 after saline; between-condition post hoc contrasts are marked p < .05 at 230 minutes and p ≤ .001 at 24, 48 and 72 hours.

key_findings.finding: Baseline HDRS was 33.0 (SD 6.7) before ketamine and 26.9 (SD 5.8) before saline (paired t test, p = 0.10). The second test day began lower than the first by 10.3 points (SD 9.0) in those given ketamine first and by 3.0 points (SD 7.5) in those given saline first (p = .29).
key_findings.note: A 10-point lower start to the saline day after ketamine is what carryover of the ketamine effect across a washout of at least 1 week would produce; the paper does not discuss it.

key_findings.finding: BDI: ketamine day 29.5 (SD 8.2) at baseline and 16.8 (SD 10.5) at the final rating; saline day 23.0 (SD 8.2) and 25.2 (SD 6.0); drug × time F = 5.7 (df 8,48), p = .0001; drug F = .007, p = .94; time F = 1.63, p = .21. Order effects examined post hoc were not significant for HDRS or BDI (p > .3).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (continued from p. 352), left column

key_findings.finding: Response (a 50% or greater HDRS fall during the 3-day follow-up): 4 of 8 after ketamine (decreases of 7, 30, 45, 47, 52, 52, 63 and 83%) against 1 of 8 after saline (decreases of 3, 6, 7, 8 and 74%; three people 4, 22 and 33% above baseline); Fisher exact p > .05.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: two-sided Fisher exact p = 0.28; difference 37.5 percentage points, 95% CI about −7 to 68 (Newcombe, treating conditions as independent). The counts use 8 people per condition, not the 7 completers of the ANOVAs.

key_findings.finding: Mood improvement after ketamine returned to baseline (clinical impression and HDRS within 5 points of baseline) 1 to 2 weeks after the infusion; one exception, whose HDRS went from 41 at baseline to 7 on day 3, was still at 15 two weeks after the infusion when he started antidepressant medication.
key_findings.note: The stated rating schedule ends at 72 hours (p. 352), so these later observations are outside it; how and when they were made is not described.

key_findings.finding: Self-rated 'high' (VAS): condition × time F = 16.9 (df 4,24), p = .0001; scores returned to baseline by 110 minutes after infusion; every patient reached a maximum of at least 50 mm on the ketamine day and none rose at all on the saline day.
key_findings.note: Figure 1, middle panel (p. 352; editors' reading, approximate): mean peak about 83 mm at the 10-minute rating, about 45 at 40 minutes and about 13 at 80 minutes.

key_findings.finding: BPRS positive symptoms: the text says ketamine produced significantly greater BPRS scores, especially positive symptoms, but the condition × time (F = 4.14, df 5,30, p = .068), time (p = .06) and condition (p = .10) effects on BPRS-positive scores were not significant; the figure legend gives p = .07 for the interaction.
key_findings.note: Figure 1, bottom panel (editors' reading, approximate): mean score about 4.5 at baseline, about 8.7 at 10 and 40 minutes and back to about 4.5 by 110 minutes after ketamine; about 4 throughout after saline; between-condition contrasts marked p ≤ .01 at 10 and 40 minutes.

key_findings.finding: Changes in BPRS or VAS-high scores did not correlate with the percentage fall in HDRS (R² < .05, p > .65).

Comparing baseline with final scores on individual HDRS items after ketamine: depressed mood (paired t test, p = .0025), suicidality (p = .02), helplessness (p = .008) and worthlessness (p = .015) decreased, uncorrected for multiple comparisons; no HDRS item improved significantly after saline.

The authors state that patients readily told the active infusion from placebo by its perceptual disturbances and 'high', and that this limit on the blind may have biased reporting by diminishing placebo effects.

The authors conclude that clinical use of this strategy may be limited by the psychotomimetic effects and potential for abuse of many NMDA antagonists, and propose testing antagonists without psychotomimetic properties (memantine, eliprodil, 1-aminocyclopropanecarboxylic acid).

reporting_issues.issue: The condition main effects are printed with df 1,30 (HDRS), 1,48 (BDI), 1,24 (VAS-high) and 1,30 (BPRS-positive). In a within-person ANOVA of 7 completers the error df for condition is 6, and the printed p values match df 1,6: for example VAS-high F = 26.3 gives p = .002 with df 1,6 against about .00003 with df 1,24, and BPRS F = 3.71 gives p = .10 with df 1,6 against .064 with df 1,30 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The df are misprinted, not the tests; claims should quote F and p, not the printed df.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that ketamine produced significantly greater BPRS scores, especially positive symptoms, while all three BPRS-positive tests in the same paragraph are non-significant (p = .068, .06, .10) and the Figure 1 legend gives p = .07; BPRS total scores are not reported. The Discussion then takes BPRS increases as evidence of 'profound' cognitive deficits, although no cognitive measure was taken.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims may not describe the BPRS rise in this study as significant or cite it for cognitive effects; the starred contrasts at 10 and 40 minutes follow a non-significant interaction.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall baseline difference (33.0 before ketamine against 26.9 before saline, paired p = 0.10) cannot be reproduced from the order-specific differences in the next sentence (10.3 and 3.0 points), and the paper does not say how many completers had each order or on which sample each baseline mean was computed. Editors' calculation: the overall difference is 6.1 points, while for 7 completers the order-specific values give a mean difference of 4.6 points if 4 had ketamine first, or 2.7 if 3 did.
reporting_issues.consequence: The baseline imbalance cannot be quantified exactly; it may come from different samples (8 per condition) than the 7-person ANOVA.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 marks the between-condition HDRS contrasts at 24, 48 and 72 hours as p ≤ .001, and the method of the contrasts is described only as Huynh-Feldt adjusted. Editors' reading and calculation (approximate): at 72 hours the plotted means differ by about 13 points with SEMs of about 4.1 and 4.5; a paired t test with df 6 would need a within-person correlation of about 0.87 between the two days' changes to reach p = .001, and an unpaired comparison gives p of about .05.
reporting_issues.consequence: The starred time-point contrasts probably used a pooled error term and overstate the precision; claims should rest on the interaction (p = .02) and the response counts, not on the stars.

reporting_issues.issue: Response is counted in 8 people per condition (including the 2 who completed only one day), while every other analysis uses the 7 completers; and response is defined only as a 50% fall 'during the 3-day follow-up period', not at a fixed time.
reporting_issues.consequence: Response may have been taken at each person's best rating, which favours the condition with larger fluctuations; the denominators differ between analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 plots the first post-baseline HDRS rating at about 40 minutes on the time axis, level with the 40-minute VAS and BPRS ratings, whereas the Methods schedule the HDRS at 80 minutes after the start of infusion (the BDI, not the HDRS, at 40 minutes).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the timing of the earliest HDRS rating is uncertain, which does not affect the 24-to-72-hour results.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes 'seven subjects with major depression', but the sample included one person with bipolar disorder, depressed; whether that person was among the 7 completers is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysed sample's diagnoses are not fully known.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Berman_2000_AntidepressantEffects.pdf: printed pp. 351–354, the whole brief report (abstract, methods, results, Figure 1 and its legend, discussion, funding note, references); born-digital PDF; every number checked on the rendered pages (150 dpi, Figure 1 at 300 dpi); no supplement; no conflict statement.
